items.title: Successive percentage change in a service contract

learning.concept: Apply each percentage change to the current value, not the original value.
learning.mental_model: Percentage changes are multipliers. A 12% increase multiplies by 1.12; a 10% reduction then multiplies the new amount by 0.90.
learning.why_this_matters: Service operations, invoices, project budgets and staffing costs often change in stages. Treating two successive percentage changes as a simple addition or subtraction gives the wrong final amount and can distort estimates.
real_world: A support contract receives an annual rate revision and then a separate negotiated discount.
A project estimate changes after a scope increase and a later cost-saving adjustment.
learning.learning_objective: Calculate the net effect of two or more successive percentage changes and explain why the base changes after each step.

recognition_signals: The prompt describes an increase and a later decrease (or multiple revisions).
Each change applies to the amount after the previous change.
anti_patterns: Adding 12% and subtracting 10% as if both use the same starting base.
Assuming equal percentage increase and decrease cancel each other.
tradeoffs: Multipliers scale to any number of sequential revisions; a base-100 worked example is easier for mental arithmetic.
Exact fractions preserve precision; round only at the final currency or percentage display.

assistance.hint_1: Start with a convenient base such as 100 units so each percentage has a visible monetary value.
assistance.hint_2: After the 12% increase, use the new amount as the base for the 10% reduction.
assistance.hint_3: Compute 100 × 1.12 × 0.90. Compare the result with 100 to find the net percentage change.
common_mistakes: Using 100 as the base for both percentages.
Subtracting 10 from 12 and reporting a 2% increase.
Reporting the final amount as the percentage change.

constraints: Use a positive starting value.
State both the final amount and the net percentage change.

test_cases.input: Starting amount 100; increase 12%; then decrease 10%.
Starting amount 500; decrease 20%; then increase 25%.

rubric.criterion: states net change relative to original

provenance.note: Original Bountycode candidate. The item is not an official or reported company question. Its skill alignment is pattern-relevant to published numerical/cognitive assessment categories.

items.problem:
A managed-services contract has a base monthly value of ₹100,000. A rate revision increases it by 12%. After the revised amount is calculated, the customer receives a 10% reduction on that revised amount. What is the final monthly value, and what is the net percentage change from the original value? Choose the one correct result.
A. ₹102,000; 2% increase
B. ₹100,800; 0.8% increase
C. ₹98,000; 2% decrease
D. ₹100,000; no change

Example check: use ₹100 as the starting amount before applying the same sequence.

worked_reasoning: Start with ₹100,000.
Reduce the revised amount by 10%: ₹112,000 × 0.90 = ₹100,800.
Compare with the original: ₹800 ÷ ₹100,000 × 100 = 0.8% increase.

distractor_analysis.A: Treats the changes as a simple 12% − 10% = 2% increase.
distractor_analysis.C: Uses the wrong base or applies the reduction before the increase.
distractor_analysis.D: Assumes the two changes cancel; they are applied to different bases.

items.title: Combined work rates

learning.concept: Convert completion times into rates before combining workers or machines.
learning.mental_model: Time describes how long one worker needs for the whole job; rate describes the fraction of the job completed per day. Independent simultaneous work adds rates, not days.
learning.why_this_matters: Support teams, migration teams and batch-processing jobs often work in parallel. Estimating combined throughput from rates helps avoid the common error of adding completion times or averaging them without justification.
real_world: Two engineers handle independent parts of a migration and their daily throughput can be combined when work is divisible.
Two batch jobs process independent records in parallel, so total throughput is the sum of their processing rates.
learning.learning_objective: Find combined completion time for independent constant-rate workers and solve for a missing worker rate.

recognition_signals: Two or more workers or machines work simultaneously on the same divisible job.
The prompt gives individual completion times or rates.
anti_patterns: Adding the number of days instead of adding work per day.
Taking the arithmetic mean of completion times without deriving a rate.
tradeoffs: Adding rates is valid for independent simultaneous work; averaging completion times is not a substitute.
Fraction arithmetic keeps the result exact; decimal rates can be faster when the values are simple.

assistance.hint_1: If A finishes one job in 12 days, write A's one-day rate as 1/12 of the job.
assistance.hint_2: Write B's rate in the same units and add the fractions to get the combined daily rate.
assistance.hint_3: For A = 12 days and B = 18 days, the rate is 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 job per day; take the reciprocal to get days.
common_mistakes: Adding 12 + 18 days.
Stopping at the combined rate instead of taking its reciprocal.
Assuming workers have identical efficiency when the question does not say so.

constraints: Assume constant rates and independent work unless stated otherwise.
Express the final time in days.

test_cases.input: A finishes in 12 days; B finishes in 18 days; both work together.
A finishes in 8 days; B finishes in 8 days; both work together.

rubric.criterion: converts each time to a rate

provenance.note: Original numerical aptitude practice. Broad pattern relevance only; not an employer-published question.

items.problem:
Two independent engineers are assigned equivalent portions of a migration task. Engineer A would complete the entire task alone in 12 days; Engineer B would complete it alone in 18 days. If both work at their usual constant rates together, how long do they need to finish one task?
A. 6 days
B. 7.2 days
C. 15 days
D. 30 days

Assume work is divisible, both start together, and neither blocks the other.

worked_reasoning: A completes 1/12 of the task per day.
B completes 1/18 of the task per day.
Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36 task per day.

distractor_analysis.A: Adds the rates incorrectly or uses a rough mental shortcut.
distractor_analysis.C: Averages 12 and 18 days, which is not valid for parallel work.
distractor_analysis.D: Adds the individual completion times and ignores parallel execution.

items.title: Service desk data interpretation

learning.concept: Read a table precisely, calculate totals and ratios, and distinguish a weighted rate from an unweighted average.
learning.mental_model: Every question has a denominator. Identify whether the denominator is a total volume, a subgroup, or a number of teams before calculating a percentage.
learning.why_this_matters: Operations and service-delivery roles use tables to track incidents, SLA performance, ticket volumes and backlog. Good analysts calculate the correct denominator and explain what the number means instead of reporting an isolated percentage.
real_world: A service desk compares incoming incident volumes and first-response performance across support queues.
A delivery manager combines counts from several teams to measure the overall share of tickets resolved within SLA.
learning.learning_objective: Calculate totals, averages, subgroup percentages and weighted overall rates from a table, then interpret what the values do and do not show.

recognition_signals: A table contains counts for multiple teams, categories or periods.
The question asks for a percentage, difference, average or total across rows.
anti_patterns: Averaging percentages when group sizes differ.
Using resolved tickets as the denominator when the question asks for a resolution rate among received tickets.
Rounding too early and choosing an answer based on a close approximation.
tradeoffs: A weighted overall rate reflects ticket volume; an unweighted team average answers a different question.
Exact counts should be summed before rounding rates; early rounding can change a close option.

assistance.hint_1: Read the table headings first. For a resolution rate, the denominator is tickets received, not tickets resolved.
assistance.hint_2: Add the received and resolved counts separately before calculating an overall rate.
assistance.hint_3: The total received is 600 and total resolved is 505, so the overall rate is 505 ÷ 600 × 100 ≈ 84.17%.
common_mistakes: Averaging the five team percentages instead of weighting by ticket count.
Subtracting resolved from received incorrectly.
Reporting a difference in percentage points as a percentage change.

constraints: Use the dataset exactly as shown.
Round percentages to two decimal places only when needed.

test_cases.input: Received counts: 120,150,90,140,100. Find total received.
Resolved counts: 108,120,63,119,95. Find overall resolved percentage.
Team C received 90 and resolved 63. Find its resolution rate.

rubric.criterion: interprets the metric with correct units

provenance.note: Original table and questions composed for Bountycode. The broad quantitative/cognitive relevance is pattern-relevant; these are not official employer questions.

items.problem:
A service desk records the following April incident volumes:

| Team | Tickets received | Tickets resolved within SLA |
|---|---:|---:|
| A | 120 | 108 |
| B | 150 | 120 |
| C | 90 | 63 |
| D | 140 | 119 |
| E | 100 | 95 |

Question 1: What is the total number of tickets received?
A. 500  B. 550  C. 600  D. 650

Question 2: What is the overall percentage resolved within SLA?
A. 80.00%  B. 82.50%  C. 84.17%  D. 88.00%

Question 3: Which team has the highest within-SLA resolution rate?
A. A  B. B  C. D  D. E

Question 4: How many tickets were not resolved within SLA across all teams?
A. 85  B. 90  C. 95  D. 105

Example: Team C's rate is 63 ÷ 90 × 100 = 70%.

calculation_notes: Total resolved = 108 + 120 + 63 + 119 + 95 = 505. Overall rate = 505/600 × 100 = 84.1666…%, which rounds to 84.17%.
Team rates: A 90%, B 80%, C 70%, D 85%, E 95%. Team E is highest; option D in Question 3.

distractor_analysis.A: Treats the total as a smaller subtotal or omits a row.
distractor_analysis.B: Rounds before combining or uses an incorrect denominator.
distractor_analysis.D: Confuses an unweighted average of team rates with the overall weighted rate.

items.title: Syllogism: avoid the converse trap
items.canonical_problem: Syllogism with universal and particular statements

learning.concept: Treat each statement as a set relationship and accept only conclusions that must be true in every arrangement satisfying the premises.
learning.mental_model: A statement that all members of A are in B does not say that all members of B are in A. Particular information about B does not automatically tell us anything about A.
learning.why_this_matters: Reasoning assessments reward conclusions that follow strictly from given information. In support and analysis work, the same discipline prevents a plausible assumption from being treated as a proven fact.
real_world: A support workflow may require every priority-one incident to be escalated, but not every escalated incident is priority one.
A report may state that all certified testers completed training; that does not imply every trained employee is certified.
learning.learning_objective: Translate all/some/no statements into set relationships and reject conclusions that reverse an implication or invent an overlap.

recognition_signals: The prompt uses words such as all, some, none or only.
A conclusion reverses the direction of an 'all A are B' statement.
The conclusion claims an overlap that the premises never establish.
anti_patterns: Assuming 'all A are B' means 'all B are A'.
Assuming two subsets overlap because they share a larger superset.
Using real-world beliefs instead of the given premises.
tradeoffs: A counterexample is efficient for disproving a conclusion that must follow; a Venn diagram helps visualize all valid arrangements.
Strict premise-based reasoning is safer than importing real-world assumptions about the groups.

assistance.hint_1: Write the first premise as a one-way containment: Analysts ⊆ Graduates.
assistance.hint_2: The second premise says some Graduates are Coders. It does not specify where those Coders sit inside the Graduate set.
assistance.hint_3: Imagine Analysts and Coders as two separate groups inside Graduates. That arrangement satisfies both premises while containing no Analyst-Coder overlap.
common_mistakes: Reversing an implication.
Confusing some with all.
Assuming two subsets overlap because both belong to a common superset.

constraints: Use only the stated premises.
A conclusion follows only if it is true in every valid arrangement.

test_cases.input: All analysts are graduates. Some graduates are coders. Conclusion: Some analysts are coders.
No archived ticket is active. Ticket X is archived. Conclusion: Ticket X is not active.

rubric.criterion: models the direction of each set relation
uses a valid counterexample or proof

provenance.note: Original syllogism item. Pattern alignment is broad reasoning preparation, not a company-specific question claim.

items.problem:
Premises:
1. All analysts are graduates.
2. Some graduates are coders.

Conclusion: Some analysts are coders.

Choose the correct evaluation.
A. The conclusion definitely follows.
B. The conclusion definitely does not follow in any possible arrangement.
C. The conclusion does not necessarily follow from the premises.
D. The premises contradict each other.

worked_reasoning: Premise 1 places every analyst inside the graduate set.
Premise 2 says at least one graduate is a coder, but it does not say that graduate is an analyst.
A valid arrangement can place the coder graduate outside the analyst subset.
Therefore an analyst-coder overlap is possible but not guaranteed.

distractor_analysis.A: Assumes the known coder graduate must be an analyst.
distractor_analysis.B: Overstates the result: the premises allow analysts and coders to overlap, but do not require it.

items.title: Reading inference without overclaiming

learning.concept: Choose an inference that is supported by the passage while avoiding stronger claims than the evidence allows.
learning.mental_model: A good inference sits one step beyond the sentence, not three steps beyond it. It connects clues without inventing causes, motives or outcomes.
learning.why_this_matters: Client updates, incident summaries and technical documentation often contain incomplete information. Professionals must distinguish what is known, what is suggested and what still needs confirmation.
real_world: A support analyst should not tell a client an outage is resolved until monitoring confirms recovery.
A project update may show a milestone slipped after a dependency delay without proving the dependency was the only cause.
learning.learning_objective: Separate explicit facts from reasonable inferences and reject causal claims unsupported by the passage.

recognition_signals: The question asks what can be inferred, implied or concluded.
The passage provides observations but not a complete causal explanation.
One answer is plausible but adds a new fact not stated or supported.
anti_patterns: Treating sequence as proof of causation.
Choosing the strongest or most dramatic conclusion.
Using outside knowledge to fill gaps in the passage.
tradeoffs: A conservative inference avoids unsupported claims; a stronger causal conclusion requires explicit evidence.
Quoting textual evidence is slower than intuition but reduces over-interpretation.

assistance.hint_1: Underline the facts the passage explicitly states before evaluating the answer choices.
assistance.hint_2: Ask which option is supported by all the clues without adding a new cause or future prediction.
assistance.hint_3: The passage says delays persisted after staffing increased. It supports the conclusion that more staff alone did not remove the bottleneck; it does not identify the exact remaining cause.
common_mistakes: Confusing after with because of.
Assuming a single root cause when the passage lists only observations.
Selecting an answer that introduces a new event.

constraints: Answer only from the passage.
Do not assume facts that are not stated or logically implied.

test_cases.input: A team increased staffing from four to six people. The queue fell slightly, but average resolution time remained above target.
test_cases.expected: More staffing alone did not bring resolution time to target.

test_cases.input: Attendance rose after a schedule change; no other evidence is supplied.
test_cases.expected: Attendance rose after the change; causation is not established.

provenance.note: Original passage and question. Broad verbal/communication practice only; not copied from employer assessments.

items.problem:
Passage:
A service team added two analysts to its evening shift after the unresolved ticket queue grew for three weeks. During the next week, the queue fell from 240 tickets to 205. However, the median resolution time remained above the service target. The report does not identify the exact cause of the remaining delay.

Which conclusion is best supported?
A. Adding analysts caused the entire queue problem to disappear.
B. The queue became smaller, but the service target was still not being met.
C. The new analysts were less productive than the previous team.
D. The ticket queue will continue to fall in the next month.

worked_reasoning: The passage explicitly states the queue dropped from 240 to 205.
It also states median resolution time remained above target.
It does not prove the staffing change caused the reduction or explain the remaining delay.
It does not predict what will happen next month.

distractor_analysis.A: Contradicts the stated fact that median resolution remained above target.
distractor_analysis.C: Invents a judgement about the new analysts that is not in the passage.
distractor_analysis.D: Predicts a future trend without evidence.

items.title: Write a clear professional status email

learning.concept: A professional status email gives the reader context, current state, impact, next action and a specific request.
learning.mental_model: The reader should be able to answer five questions quickly: what is this about, what changed, what is the impact, what happens next, and what do you need from me?
learning.why_this_matters: Entry-level engineers and analysts communicate with teammates, clients and managers during handovers, incidents and delivery updates. Clear writing reduces unnecessary follow-up and prevents a status message from sounding defensive or vague.
real_world: A developer communicates a blocker and revised estimate to a project lead.
A support analyst hands over an unresolved incident with impact, actions taken and the next owner.
learning.learning_objective: Choose an appropriate subject line, state facts neutrally, include a concrete next step and make a polite, specific request.

recognition_signals: The reader needs an update or action rather than a long narrative.
A deadline, blocker or ownership handoff must be clear.
The message should separate confirmed facts from estimates.
anti_patterns: Using vague subjects such as 'Hi' or 'Important'.
Blaming another team or using emotional language.
Saying 'will update soon' without a time or next action.
tradeoffs: Concise writing reduces reading time; too much compression can omit ownership, impact or the actual request.
A specific next-update time is useful when known; inventing an ETA creates an avoidable commitment.

assistance.hint_1: Choose a subject that names the project or incident and the requested action.
assistance.hint_2: Use short paragraphs: context, current status and impact, then next action/request.
assistance.hint_3: State the exact deliverable and when you will provide it; use neutral language and avoid assigning blame.
common_mistakes: Missing the ask.
No date or owner for the next action.
Promising a resolution time that has not been confirmed.

constraints: Use neutral, professional language.
Do not invent a confirmed resolution time.
Include one specific request or next action.

test_cases.input: A deployment is blocked by a failing integration test. The team is investigating and expects to share a revised estimate by 3 PM.
test_cases.expected: Subject, factual blocker, impact, current action, and time-bound next update.

test_cases.input: You need a reviewer to approve a pull request before a release cut-off.
test_cases.expected: Clear request with PR context and deadline.

rubric.criterion: time-bound request or update where justified

provenance.note: Original professional communication practice. It is not represented as a named employer assessment item.

items.problem:
You are a junior developer on a release team. A deployment is blocked because an integration test fails in the staging environment. The team is investigating. You have not confirmed the root cause or a resolution time. You can provide the next update by 3:00 PM.

Which email is the best professional update?

A. Subject: Important. The deployment is broken because the other team did not do their job. We will fix it soon.
B. Subject: Staging deployment blocked — integration test failure. The release is currently on hold while we investigate the failing integration test. I will share the findings and a revised estimate by 3:00 PM. Please let me know if the release cut-off has changed.
C. Subject: Hi. There is an issue. Please check.
D. Subject: Deployment solved. The test is failing but we will definitely finish before lunch.

worked_reasoning: The subject names the status and specific cause currently observed.
The message separates the known failure from the unconfirmed root cause.
It states the impact (release on hold), current action (investigation) and a time-bound next update.
The final sentence makes a polite, relevant request without assigning blame.

distractor_analysis.A: Blames another team and promises a fix without evidence.
distractor_analysis.C: Does not provide enough context or an actionable request.
distractor_analysis.D: Claims the issue is solved and guarantees an unconfirmed deadline.

items.title: Trace a nested loop with a changing inner bound

learning.concept: A nested loop executes the inner body a number of times determined by the current outer-loop value.
learning.mental_model: For each outer-loop value, reset the inner-loop variable and trace every iteration before moving to the next outer value.
learning.why_this_matters: Programming-logic and pseudocode assessments often test whether a candidate can maintain variable state across nested loops. A disciplined trace also helps engineers debug counters, retry logic and batch-processing code.
real_world: A batch processor loops over each customer and then over that customer's records.
A test runner iterates over suites and then over individual test cases within each suite.
learning.learning_objective: Produce an iteration table for nested loops, calculate loop-body execution count and track an accumulator without skipping or duplicating iterations.

recognition_signals: An inner loop uses the current outer variable in its limit.
An accumulator changes inside the inner loop.
The question asks for a final printed value or number of iterations.
anti_patterns: Assuming the inner loop has the same number of iterations each time.
Failing to reset the inner variable for each outer iteration.
Updating an accumulator only once per outer iteration when the statement is inside the inner loop.
tradeoffs: A row-by-row state table is reliable for short traces; formulas are faster only after loop bounds are understood.
Counting body executions differs from counting condition checks, so name the quantity being asked.

assistance.hint_1: List the outer values first: i = 1, 2, 3. For each one, the inner loop starts again at j = 0.
assistance.hint_2: Write one row per body execution and update total by i + j each time.
assistance.hint_3: The contributions are 1; then 2 and 3; then 3, 4 and 5. Add them to get 18.
common_mistakes: Keeping j from the previous outer iteration.
Using j <= i instead of j < i.
Updating total with i only and ignoring j.
Counting loop-condition checks as body executions.

constraints: Outer loop: i takes values 1, 2, 3.
Inner loop: j starts at 0 and continues while j < i.
The body adds i + j to total.

test_cases.input: total=0; for i=1..3: for j=0..i-1: total += i+j
Count body executions for i=1..4 with j=0..i-1.

provenance.note: Original pseudocode-style trace candidate. Infosys HackWithInfy is a distinct coding competition; this item is broad programming-logic practice and is not an official test question.

items.problem:
Trace the following pseudocode. The inner loop starts again at zero for each outer-loop value.

```
total = 0
for i = 1 to 3:
    for j = 0 to i - 1:
        total = total + i + j
print(total)
```

What is printed?
A. 10
B. 12
C. 18
D. 21

Example trace for i=2: j takes 0 and 1, so the body adds 2 and 3.

worked_reasoning: For i=1, the inner loop runs once: add 1.
For i=2, the inner loop runs twice: add 2 then 3.
For i=3, the inner loop runs three times: add 3, then 4, then 5.

distractor_analysis.A: Misses one or more inner iterations.
distractor_analysis.B: Counts iterations but uses an incomplete accumulator update.
distractor_analysis.D: Runs the inner loop one extra time or misreads the inclusive/exclusive bound.

items.title: First non-repeating character

learning.concept: Count occurrences first, then scan the original sequence to find the first item with frequency one.
learning.mental_model: The frequency map answers how often each character occurs; the original order answers which unique character appears first. These are two separate responsibilities.
learning.why_this_matters: Frequency maps are a foundational service-level coding pattern used in log parsing, input validation and string analysis. The problem tests both a useful data structure and the discipline to preserve original order.
real_world: A log analyzer can identify the first character or token that appears only once in a record.
A text-processing utility can locate the first unique symbol while preserving the original input order.
learning.learning_objective: Implement a two-pass frequency-map solution and explain its O(n) time and O(k) auxiliary-space complexity.

recognition_signals: The prompt asks for first/earliest/leftmost item satisfying a frequency condition.
The input is a sequence where order must be preserved.
Repeated membership checks would make a nested-loop solution unnecessarily slow.
anti_patterns: Returning the first character inserted into a hash map without checking order.
Sorting the string and losing the original position.
Using a nested scan for every character without considering O(n²) work.
tradeoffs: A two-pass hash-map approach is O(n) and preserves input order; sorting loses the required order.
A fixed-size frequency array can reduce overhead for a restricted alphabet; a map handles a wider character set.

assistance.hint_1: You need both frequency and original order; do not sort the input.
assistance.hint_2: First pass: increment a count for every character. Second pass: return the first character whose count is exactly one.
assistance.hint_3: For 'swiss', counts are s:3, w:1, i:1. Scanning the original string finds 'w' before 'i'.
common_mistakes: Returning any unique character rather than the first unique character.
Treating uppercase and lowercase as equal without being asked to normalize case.
Failing to define what to return when no unique character exists.

constraints: Input contains lowercase English letters only.
Return an empty string when every character repeats.
Target time complexity O(n).

test_cases.input: swiss
aabbc
aabb

rubric.criterion: preserves original order in second pass

provenance.note: Original coding candidate. Broad array/string/hash-map pattern practice; not copied from an employer's item bank.

items.problem:
Given a string containing lowercase English letters, return the first character that appears exactly once. Return an empty string if no such character exists.

Examples:
- input: `swiss` → output: `w`
- input: `aabbc` → output: `c`
- input: `aabb` → output: `""`

What is the best general approach for O(n) time?
A. Sort the string, then select the first character
B. Count frequencies, then scan the original string in order
C. Compare every pair of characters using nested loops
D. Return the first character that is different from the final character.

algorithm: Scan the input once and increment the count for each character.
Scan the input again from left to right.
Return the first character whose count equals one; if none exists, return an empty string.
solution.space_complexity: O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters

distractor_analysis.A: Sorting changes original order, so it cannot preserve the first unique character in the input.
distractor_analysis.C: Can work but is O(n²) in the straightforward implementation.
distractor_analysis.D: A character differing from the last character does not imply that it appears exactly once.

items.title: HTTP methods and retry safety

learning.concept: Idempotency describes whether repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once.
learning.mental_model: A retry is safe only when repeating the operation does not create additional unintended state. Ask whether the request sets a target state or creates another action each time.
learning.why_this_matters: Service-company engineers maintain APIs and distributed applications where clients retry after timeouts or network failures. Understanding idempotency helps prevent duplicate orders, payments and resource creation.
real_world: A client retries a resource update after losing the response and must avoid applying the state change repeatedly.
An API gateway handles transient failures without creating duplicate resources or business transactions.
learning.learning_objective: Distinguish safe/idempotent HTTP semantics from methods that typically create new actions, and explain why an idempotency key may be required.

recognition_signals: A request may be retried after a timeout or lost response.
The operation updates a resource to a desired state rather than creating a new action.
Duplicate side effects would be harmful.
anti_patterns: Assuming every POST is automatically safe to retry.
Confusing an identical response with an idempotent state change.
Ignoring business-level idempotency for payment or order creation.
tradeoffs: PUT expresses a desired resource state and is intended to be idempotent; POST often represents creation or an action.
An idempotency key adds business-level retry safety for POST but requires server-side persistence and expiry policy.

assistance.hint_1: Think about the server-side effect, not just the HTTP response body.
assistance.hint_2: Repeating a PUT to set the same resource representation should not create another resource or increment a counter.
assistance.hint_3: For an order-creation POST, use a unique idempotency key and persist the key/result so a retry can return the original outcome instead of creating another order.
common_mistakes: Claiming POST is always idempotent.
Assuming every PUT request has no side effects in every application.
Using retries without an idempotency strategy for payments.

constraints: Use standard HTTP semantics; application-specific safeguards may add stronger guarantees.
Distinguish protocol intent from implementation defects.

test_cases.input: Client retries PUT /users/42 with the same desired representation.
Client retries POST /payments without a deduplication key.
test_cases.expected: Not generally safe; may create duplicate payment actions.

rubric.criterion: defines idempotency as same intended effect
mentions business-level deduplication for retryable POST

provenance.note: Original technical-interview scenario. Company mappings are role-relevant preparation hypotheses, not published company question claims.

items.problem:
An application sends `POST /payments` to create a payment. The network times out before the client receives a response. The client retries the exact same request. Which design best prevents a duplicate payment?

A. Assume POST is idempotent and retry without tracking the request.
B. Attach a unique idempotency key and persist the outcome so repeated requests with that key return the original result.
C. Change the HTTP method to GET but keep the request body.
D. Retry the request with a new random key each time.

worked_reasoning: A timeout does not prove the server failed to process the first request.
POST is not generally idempotent, so a second request may create another payment.
A stable idempotency key lets the server recognize the same logical operation and return the stored outcome.
A new key for each retry defeats deduplication.

distractor_analysis.A: Assumes a guarantee POST does not provide by default.
distractor_analysis.C: Misuses GET and does not fix payment creation semantics.
distractor_analysis.D: Creates a new identity for the retry, so it cannot be deduplicated as the same operation.

items.title: Boundary-value testing

learning.concept: Boundary-value analysis selects tests at, just below and just above input limits because defects often occur where conditions change.
learning.mental_model: If an input is valid from 1 through 100, test the edges: 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101—not just a typical middle value.
learning.why_this_matters: Entry-level engineers often need to validate form inputs, API parameters and business rules. Boundary-focused test design finds off-by-one errors that happy-path examples miss.
real_world: A registration API validates age or quantity ranges before writing data.
A report filter accepts page sizes within a documented range and must reject values outside it.
learning.learning_objective: Construct boundary test sets and explain how each test distinguishes inclusive and exclusive limits.

recognition_signals: The specification gives a minimum or maximum value.
The implementation uses <, <=, > or >= conditions.
A value changes from valid to invalid at a defined boundary.
anti_patterns: Testing only ordinary mid-range values.
Testing the minimum and maximum but not just outside them.
Ignoring empty, null or one-item inputs when the specification permits them.
tradeoffs: Boundary-value analysis is compact and high-yield; equivalence partitioning adds representative tests from each valid/invalid class.
A small boundary set is more targeted than random mid-range values, but it does not replace broader integration testing.

assistance.hint_1: Write down the inclusive valid range exactly as stated before choosing tests.
assistance.hint_2: For each boundary, select the value itself and the nearest value on either side.
assistance.hint_3: For 1 ≤ quantity ≤ 100, include 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101; then add null/empty only if the API contract defines them.
common_mistakes: Testing 1 and 100 but not 0 or 101.
Assuming whether an endpoint is inclusive without reading the specification.
Mixing boundary analysis with random testing.

constraints: Valid quantity is an integer from 1 through 100 inclusive.
Do not assume behavior for non-integer values unless stated.

test_cases.input: quantity must satisfy 1 <= quantity <= 100
test_cases.expected: 0 invalid; 1 valid; 2 valid; 99 valid; 100 valid; 101 invalid

test_cases.input: page_size must satisfy 1 <= page_size < 51

rubric.criterion: tests both sides of each boundary

provenance.note: Original testing fundamentals candidate. This is role-relevant preparation rather than a claim about a specific employer's test.

items.problem:
An API accepts `quantity` as an integer from 1 through 100, inclusive. Which set gives the most useful boundary-value coverage?

A. 10, 20, 30, 40
B. 1, 100
C. 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101
D. 50, 60, 70, 80, 90

worked_reasoning: The valid range is inclusive: 1 ≤ quantity ≤ 100.
Test 0 just below the lower boundary, 1 at the lower boundary and 2 just above it.
Test 99 just below the upper boundary, 100 at the upper boundary and 101 just above it.
This detects common off-by-one and comparison-operator errors.

distractor_analysis.A: Typical valid values do not exercise the validity transition.
distractor_analysis.B: Tests the endpoints but not just outside or just inside them.

items.title: Average speed over equal distances
items.canonical_problem: Average speed with unequal segment speeds

learning.concept: For equal distances, average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the arithmetic mean of the two speeds.
learning.mental_model: Imagine the same road segment travelled twice. The slower segment consumes more time, so it has more influence on the average.
learning.why_this_matters: Transport, field-support and delivery estimates combine speed and time. The arithmetic mean of two speeds is only valid in special cases such as equal travel times, not equal distances.
real_world: A field engineer drives the same 60 km route outward and back at different speeds.
A service delivery estimate compares travel legs with different speeds but known distances.
learning.learning_objective: Calculate average speed from total distance and total time, and identify when arithmetic averaging is invalid.

recognition_signals: The prompt gives equal distances at different speeds.
The question asks for one average over the complete journey.
anti_patterns: Taking the arithmetic mean of speeds without checking travel times.
Averaging segment times instead of adding them.
tradeoffs: Total distance/time is universally safe when both are known.
A reciprocal-rate formula can be faster for exactly equal distances.

assistance.hint_1: Write the same distance for each leg and find each leg's travel time.
assistance.hint_2: Add the two distances and add the two travel times separately.
assistance.hint_3: For 60 km at 30 km/h and 60 km at 60 km/h, time is 2 h + 1 h = 3 h; total distance is 120 km; average = 40 km/h.
common_mistakes: Using distance as if it were time.
Taking the arithmetic mean of speeds.
Dropping units while adding hours and kilometres.

constraints: Both legs cover the same distance.
Assume constant speed on each leg.

test_cases.input: 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 60 km/h

rubric.criterion: adds total distance and total time

provenance.note: Original synthetic item. Numerical reasoning alignment is broad and pattern-relevant only; not an official employer question.

items.problem:
A field engineer drives 60 km to a customer site at 30 km/h and returns over the same 60 km route at 60 km/h. What is the average speed for the complete 120 km journey?
A. 45 km/h
B. 40 km/h
C. 42 km/h
D. 50 km/h

worked_reasoning: Outbound time = 60/30 = 2 hours.
Return time = 60/60 = 1 hour.
Total distance = 120 km and total time = 3 hours.
Average speed = 120/3 = 40 km/h.

distractor_analysis.A: Arithmetic mean of the two speeds; that would correspond to equal travel times, not equal distances.
distractor_analysis.D: Does not follow from total distance divided by total time.

items.title: Direction reasoning on a coordinate grid

learning.concept: Represent each movement as a signed change on horizontal and vertical axes, then compute the final displacement.
learning.mental_model: North increases the vertical coordinate, south decreases it, east increases horizontal position and west decreases it.
learning.why_this_matters: Direction questions test careful state updates. The same coordinate method is used in navigation, grid-based systems and tracking movement in a sequence of operations.
real_world: An engineer traces a robot's movement through a warehouse grid.
A support analyst interprets a sequence of location changes in a simple simulation.
learning.learning_objective: Track a sequence of cardinal-direction moves and distinguish final displacement from total path length.

recognition_signals: The prompt gives several north/south/east/west moves.
The question asks for the final position or straight-line distance from the start.
anti_patterns: Adding all movement magnitudes without cancelling opposite directions.
Confusing total path length with displacement.
Reversing the sign of west or south.
tradeoffs: A coordinate pair provides exact final position; Pythagoras gives straight-line distance.
A hand-drawn compass sketch is intuitive; coordinates are easier to audit.

assistance.hint_1: Set the starting point to (0,0) and write east/west as horizontal changes.
assistance.hint_2: Add north and south movements separately, then east and west movements.
assistance.hint_3: North 5 then south 2 gives y=3; east 3 then west 1 gives x=2; final point is (2,3).
common_mistakes: Treating north and south as the same direction.
Reporting total path length when asked for displacement.
Forgetting that opposite movements cancel.

constraints: Start at (0,0).
North/east are positive; south/west are negative.

provenance.note: Original direction-reasoning item; broad cognitive-preparation alignment only, not an employer-reported question.

items.problem:
A technician starts at the service desk. They walk 5 blocks north, 3 blocks east, 2 blocks south, then 1 block west. Relative to the starting point, where are they?
A. 2 blocks west and 3 north
B. 2 blocks east and 3 north
C. 3 blocks east and 2 north
D. 2 blocks east and 7 north

worked_reasoning: North/south: +5 − 2 = +3.
East/west: +3 − 1 = +2.
The final coordinate is (2,3), which is northeast of the start.

distractor_analysis.A: Reverses the sign of the net east-west movement.
distractor_analysis.C: Confuses the remaining north and east values.
distractor_analysis.D: Adds north and south instead of subtracting opposing movements.

items.title: Subject–verb agreement with intervening phrases
items.canonical_problem: Find the true subject before choosing the verb

learning.concept: The verb agrees with the grammatical subject, not with a nearby noun inside a modifying phrase.
learning.mental_model: Temporarily remove phrases such as 'together with', 'along with' or 'as well as' to reveal the subject and its number.
learning.why_this_matters: Clear subject–verb agreement matters in project emails, incident summaries and technical documentation. Long noun phrases often distract writers from the true subject.
real_world: A release note describes a list of outstanding defects with additional comments.
A project update refers to one team along with several reviewers.
learning.learning_objective: Identify the main subject in a sentence with an intervening phrase and select the matching verb.

recognition_signals: A singular or plural subject is followed by an 'along with' or 'together with' phrase.
The nearest noun has a different number from the main subject.
anti_patterns: Matching the verb to the nearest noun.
Treating 'together with' as if it were 'and'.
tradeoffs: Removing the intervening phrase reveals the subject quickly.
A full sentence diagram is more detailed but slower for a short assessment item.

assistance.hint_1: Find the main noun phrase that the sentence is actually about.
assistance.hint_2: Temporarily remove 'together with two notes' and read the remaining sentence.
assistance.hint_3: The subject is 'The list' (singular), so the correct verb is 'is'.
common_mistakes: Choosing the plural noun 'notes' as the subject.
Treating 'together with' as a coordinating conjunction.

constraints: Use standard present-tense agreement.
The sentence has one main subject.

test_cases.input: The list of tickets, together with two notes, ___ on the desk.

provenance.note: Original grammar item. Broad verbal-ability preparation, not an official or candidate-reported question.

items.problem:
Choose the grammatically correct verb: "The list of unresolved tickets, together with two review notes, ___ on the desk."
A. are
B. were
C. is
D. have been

worked_reasoning: The main subject is 'The list'.
The phrase 'of unresolved tickets' describes the list; it is not the subject.
'Together with two review notes' adds information but does not make the subject plural.
A singular subject takes 'is' in this sentence.

distractor_analysis.A: Incorrectly agrees with the nearby plural noun 'tickets' or 'notes'.
distractor_analysis.B: Changes tense and number without support.
distractor_analysis.D: Uses a plural auxiliary with the singular subject.

items.title: Trace sequential array assignments
items.canonical_problem: State changes happen immediately and in order

learning.concept: Array assignments update the current state immediately; a later statement reads the updated value, not the original value.
learning.mental_model: Treat the array as a row of memory cells. After each assignment, overwrite that cell before evaluating the next statement.
learning.why_this_matters: Many pseudocode assessments test aliasing and update order. The same mental model helps debug in-place transformations and mutable state in application code.
real_world: An in-place data transformation updates fields in a record one statement at a time.
A debugging trace explains why the second assignment uses a value changed by the first.
learning.learning_objective: Trace sequential array mutations and produce the exact final array without treating assignments as simultaneous.

recognition_signals: A prompt assigns one array index using the value from another index.
A later statement reads an index modified earlier in the sequence.
anti_patterns: Treating assignments as simultaneous swaps.
Reading the original value after it has already been overwritten.
Confusing an index with an element position.
tradeoffs: A state table is safest for multi-step updates; a mental trace is faster for short sequences.
A temporary variable is needed for a true swap when values would otherwise be overwritten.

assistance.hint_1: Write the original values with their indexes before executing the first assignment.
assistance.hint_2: Apply each assignment from top to bottom and overwrite the target cell immediately.
assistance.hint_3: Starting [2,4,6], set index 0 to index 1 → [4,4,6]; set index 1 to index 2 → [4,6,6]; set index 2 to index 0 → [4,6,4].
common_mistakes: Assuming the three assignments perform a rotation automatically.
Using one-based indexing.
Failing to update the state table after each line.

constraints: Array indexing is zero-based.
Assignments execute in the written order.

test_cases.input: values=[2,4,6]; values[0]=values[1]; values[1]=values[2]; values[2]=values[0]

provenance.note: Original pseudocode state-trace item. Broad programming-logic practice; not claimed to be an employer question.

items.problem:
Given values = [2, 4, 6], execute these statements in order:

values[0] = values[1]
values[1] = values[2]
values[2] = values[0]

What is the final array?
A. [4, 6, 2]
B. [4, 6, 4]
C. [2, 6, 4]
D. [6, 4, 2]

worked_reasoning: The first statement overwrites index 0 with 4.
The second statement reads index 2 (6) and writes it to index 1.
The third statement reads the now-current index 0 (4) and writes it to index 2.
No temporary variable is used, so this is not a simultaneous rotation.

distractor_analysis.A: Would be the result of a different rotation that preserves the original value 2.
distractor_analysis.C: Does not apply the first assignment to the later reads.
distractor_analysis.D: Reorders the source and destination indexes.

items.title: Second-largest distinct array value

learning.concept: The second-largest distinct value is not necessarily the second element after sorting and may differ from the largest when duplicates occur.
learning.mental_model: Maintain the largest and second-largest distinct values while scanning. A value equal to the largest must not replace the second-largest.
learning.why_this_matters: Array scanning and duplicate handling are common building blocks in service-level coding. This problem checks loop invariants and edge-case reasoning without requiring an advanced data structure.
real_world: A monitoring report needs the runner-up distinct latency or transaction value.
A simple ranking function must skip tied duplicate maximum values.
learning.learning_objective: Return the second-largest distinct integer in one pass using O(1) extra space, and define behavior when fewer than two distinct values exist.

recognition_signals: The prompt asks for second-largest distinct rather than second position.
The input may contain duplicates or negative integers.
anti_patterns: Setting secondLargest to the previous value even when it equals largest.
Initializing both values to zero, which fails for all-negative inputs.
Returning the largest when the array contains only one distinct value.
tradeoffs: A one-pass invariant uses O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Sorting is simpler to explain but costs O(n log n) and may mutate or copy the input.

assistance.hint_1: Keep two candidates: the largest distinct value and the best distinct value below it.
assistance.hint_2: When a new value exceeds largest, shift largest down to secondLargest. Otherwise update secondLargest only if the value is distinct from largest and is larger than the current secondLargest.
assistance.hint_3: For [5,1,5,3,2], largest remains 5; the best distinct value below it becomes 3.
common_mistakes: Counting duplicate 5 as the second-largest value.
Using zero as an invalid sentinel for negative arrays.
Failing to handle arrays with fewer than two distinct values.

constraints: Input is a list of integers.
Return null if fewer than two distinct values exist.

provenance.note: Original coding candidate. Array problem-solving is pattern-relevant to broad entry-level coding preparation; not an employer question.

items.problem:
Given an integer array, return the second-largest distinct value. Return null if fewer than two distinct values exist.

Examples:
- [5,1,5,3,2] → 3
- [-8,-2,-2,-5] → -5
- [4,4,4] → null

Which invariant is most useful for a one-pass O(n) solution?
A. Keep only the last two values seen.
B. Track the largest and second-largest distinct values.
C. Sort after every insertion.
D. Count only how many times the maximum appears.

algorithm: Initialize largest and secondLargest as unset values.
For each x: if largest is unset or x > largest, move largest into secondLargest and set largest=x.
Otherwise, if x is distinct from largest and secondLargest is unset or x > secondLargest, set secondLargest=x.
Return secondLargest, or null if it was never assigned.

distractor_analysis.A: The final two elements need not be the two largest values.
distractor_analysis.C: Repeated sorting is unnecessary and not O(n).
distractor_analysis.D: The count of the maximum does not reveal the next distinct value.

items.title: Runtime method dispatch
items.canonical_problem: The actual object determines the overridden method

learning.concept: When an instance method is overridden, a call through a base-class reference dispatches to the implementation belonging to the object's runtime class.
learning.mental_model: The variable's declared type controls which members are available at compile time; the object's runtime type determines which overridden instance-method implementation runs.
learning.why_this_matters: Service-company technical interviews often test whether a candidate can explain core OOP concepts precisely. This distinction matters when reading code that uses interfaces, base classes and injected implementations.
real_world: A controller calls a service through an interface while the runtime supplies a concrete implementation.
A framework uses a base reference to invoke a subclass override.
learning.learning_objective: Predict which overridden instance method executes when a base-class reference refers to a subclass object.

recognition_signals: A base-type variable is assigned an object of a derived class.
The derived class overrides an instance method with the same signature.
anti_patterns: Choosing the method from the reference variable's declared class.
Confusing overriding with overloading or static method hiding.
Assuming every language uses identical dispatch rules for static methods.
tradeoffs: Runtime dispatch supports substitutable implementations; explicit downcasts reduce flexibility and can be unsafe.
Static overload resolution and instance-method overriding happen at different stages.

assistance.hint_1: Separate the declared reference type from the runtime object type.
assistance.hint_2: Check whether the method is an overridden instance method rather than a static or overloaded method.
assistance.hint_3: The reference is type Base, but the object is Derived; the override in Derived executes for the virtual instance call.
common_mistakes: Confusing reference type and object type.
Treating overloading as overriding.
Generalizing virtual dispatch to static methods.

constraints: Assume a language with conventional virtual dispatch for overridden instance methods (such as Java).
Both methods have the same signature.

test_cases.input: Base ref = new Derived(); ref.run(); where Derived overrides run()

rubric.criterion: distinguishes instance dispatch from static/overload resolution

provenance.note: Original OOP technical-interview practice. It reflects a general entry-level engineering skill, not an employer-published question.

worked_reasoning: The reference variable is declared as Base, so Base members determine which method can be called.
The object created at runtime is Derived.
run() is an overridden instance method, so runtime dispatch selects Derived.run().
The output is Derived.

distractor_analysis.A: Uses the declared reference type as if it selected the runtime implementation.
distractor_analysis.D: The override is valid and the reference is compatible with the subclass instance.

items.title: Collaborative Git pull-request workflow
items.canonical_problem: Isolate changes and integrate through review

learning.concept: A feature branch isolates a developer's work from the shared main branch; a pull request proposes the change for review and controlled integration.
learning.mental_model: A branch is a movable pointer to a sequence of commits. A pull request is a collaboration/review workflow around comparing one branch with another; creating the PR does not itself merge the code.
learning.why_this_matters: New engineers in service teams routinely work in shared repositories, review changes and handle merge conflicts. Understanding the workflow reduces accidental commits to main and makes code changes traceable.
real_world: Two developers work on separate features without overwriting each other's working branch.
A team requires review and CI checks before changes are integrated into the protected main branch.
learning.learning_objective: Select a safe workflow for implementing a feature collaboratively and explain the purpose of a pull request.

recognition_signals: The task changes shared application code.
A team asks for review and automated checks before integration.
anti_patterns: Committing unfinished work directly to shared main.
Assuming a pull request is already merged.
Treating a branch as a separate copy of the entire repository.
tradeoffs: Feature branches isolate parallel work; direct commits are simpler only in intentionally single-maintainer workflows.
Rebase can create a linear history; merge commits preserve an explicit branch integration point. Follow the team's convention.

assistance.hint_1: Start from an up-to-date main and create a dedicated feature branch.
assistance.hint_2: Commit focused changes on the feature branch, push it, and open a pull request targeting main.
assistance.hint_3: Review comments and CI checks must be addressed; only then can an authorized maintainer merge the PR.
common_mistakes: Pushing to the wrong branch.
Merging before review or required checks finish.
Assuming a PR automatically updates main.

constraints: Assume the repository uses pull requests and main is protected.

test_cases.input: Collaborator implements feature and must receive review before integration.
test_cases.expected: feature branch -> commits -> push -> pull request -> review/CI -> authorized merge

provenance.note: Original engineering-workflow scenario. This is general teamwork practice and not a named employer interview question.

items.problem:
A developer must add a feature to a shared repository. The team requires code review and CI checks before integration. Which sequence is safest?

A. Commit directly to main, then ask for review after deployment.
B. Create a feature branch from up-to-date main, commit and push the work, open a pull request, address review/CI findings, then merge when authorized.
C. Create a local branch but never push it; ask another developer to copy the files into main.
D. Open a pull request from main into the feature branch and assume it merges automatically.

worked_reasoning: Starting from up-to-date main reduces avoidable integration conflicts.
A feature branch isolates changes from the shared base branch.
A pull request provides a review and CI checkpoint.
The PR is merged only after required checks and review are satisfied.

distractor_analysis.A: Bypasses the review and CI policy and puts unreviewed code directly on main.
distractor_analysis.C: Breaks traceability and makes the change difficult to review or reproduce.
distractor_analysis.D: A pull request is a proposed integration, not an automatic merge.
